opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, because the analogy to software versioning is so tempting. With code, a diff is meaningful: you change a line, and that line has semantics. You can read it, you can reason about what it does, and you can merge changes from different people because the structure of the program is, more or less, aligned.

With neural networks, that breaks down in a couple of ways. The first is that individual weights don't carry meaning on their own. If I fine-tune a model and compute the element-wise difference to the original, I get a huge tensor of small changes spread across millions or billions of parameters. Technically that's a diff, but it doesn't tell me *what* changed in terms of behavior. Did the model learn a new concept? Did it forget something? Did it become more biased? You can't read that off the delta.

The second issue, which we've thought about a lot in our work on model zoos and weight-space learning, is symmetry. Neural networks have permutation symmetries: you can shuffle the neurons in a hidden layer, permute the incoming and outgoing weights accordingly, and you get exactly the same function. So two models that behave identically can look completely different in weight space, and two models that are close in weight space are only comparable if they share a common lineage, say, fine-tuned from the same checkpoint. A naive diff between two independently trained models is essentially meaningless. In software, you don't have that problem; nobody randomly reorders your functions and claims it's the same program.

And then merging is even harder. In Git, merging two branches is mostly a structural operation. In neural networks, averaging or combining weights only works under fairly specific conditions: shared initialization, being in the same loss basin, sometimes after aligning neurons first. Outside of that, you get interference and the merged model just falls apart.

So my view is that if we really want versioning for neural networks, we need representations that live closer to the function, not just raw parameters. That's part of the motivation behind learning representations of weights themselves, what we call hyper-representations, where you train a model on populations of models so it learns which directions in weight space actually matter. Then a "diff" could become something more semantic: this version is more robust, this one shifted on these classes, and so on. The software diff is a good starting point for infrastructure, but it's not the right abstraction for understanding how models evolve.

r001.rationale: The response says fine-tuning can produce small changes spread across many parameters, but does not state that a single training update can change essentially every weight.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing to understand is that a diff in software works because code has structure that a diff can exploit. Line by line, you can look at a text file and say, this line changed, this line didn't, and that gives you something meaningful. A neural network doesn't give you that. What you have are tensors, millions or billions of floating point numbers, and when you fine-tune a model or continue training it, essentially every one of those numbers changes. Not by much, maybe in the fourth or fifth decimal place, but they all move. So if you take the naive approach and compute a diff, you end up with something that is basically the same size as the model itself. You haven't gained anything in terms of storage, and you certainly haven't gained anything in terms of understanding what actually changed.

And that's the second point. In software, a diff is readable. A human can look at it and say, okay, this function was refactored, this bug was fixed. With weights, even if you had a compact representation of the change, nobody can look at a delta in the attention weights of layer seventeen and tell you what that means semantically. The meaning of a change in a network is distributed across all of the parameters, so the line-level, local notion of a change that a diff relies on just doesn't map onto how these models actually work.

There's also a practical issue with how the values are stored. Floating point numbers are noisy. If you train the same model twice with a slightly different random seed, or on different hardware, you get weights that are numerically different everywhere but functionally almost identical. A text diff would tell you that everything changed, when from the point of view of the model's behavior, nothing meaningful changed at all. So the diff is sensitive to exactly the wrong things.

That's why, in our work, we started thinking about this differently. Rather than versioning the weights as if they were source code, you have to think about what the delta between two models represents, and whether you can learn a representation of that delta, or exploit the structure of training, things like low-rank updates, sparsity in which parameters actually matter, to get something that is both compact and tells you something. Git and the whole tooling around it is wonderful for code, but it was built on an assumption about what a change looks like, and neural networks violate that assumption from the very first byte.

r001.rationale: The response says that fine-tuning or continued training changes essentially every weight, but does not state that a single training update can do so.

astra-6.text:
A software diff is useful because the code gives you a fairly direct description of what changed. With a neural network, you can compare the weights, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you what changed in its behavior.

For example, you can permute neurons in a layer and adjust the connections in the next layer, and the network still computes the same function. A weight-by-weight diff could show substantial changes even though the model’s behavior is identical. Conversely, a small change in the weights can matter a lot for particular inputs.

So the question is: what do we actually want to version? The parameters, the training process, or the learned behavior? You still want to track the code, data, and checkpoints. But to understand the difference between two models, you also need to examine their representations and their performance on meaningful inputs. A parameter diff alone doesn’t give you that.

r001.rationale: The response discusses neuron permutations and says a small weight change can affect particular inputs, but it does not state that one training update can slightly change essentially every weight.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, a software diff assumes that the location of a change tells you something meaningful about what changed. With a neural network, that relationship is much less direct. You can compare two checkpoints and see which weights have changed, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you how the behavior of the model has changed.

There are also symmetries in these networks. You can permute neurons in a layer and adjust the connections in the next layer, and you have different weight matrices representing exactly the same function. A conventional diff might show a huge change where, functionally, nothing has changed.

So we need to distinguish between differences in the parameters and differences in what the network actually does. The weights are useful information, but for meaningful versioning, we also need to look at the model’s outputs and behavior on relevant data.

r001.rationale: The response says weights can change between checkpoints, but does not state that one training update can slightly change essentially every weight.
